entries.title: Russia, Ukraine trade deadly strikes as Zelenskyy attends UNGA
entries.summary: The Russian army targeted economic infrastructure in Ukraine, while Ukraine struck an oil refinery. This comes ahead of the UN General Assembly, where President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is due to meet Trump on the sidelines.
entries.content:
Ukraine

Russia, Ukraine trade deadly strikes ahead of UNGA

September 22, 2026

The Russian army targeted economic infrastructure in Ukraine, while Ukraine struck an oil refinery. This comes ahead of the UN General Assembly, where President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is due to meet Trump on the sidelines.

Russia and Ukraine traded strikes targeting infrastructure overnight, ahead of a United Nations General Assembly where the war in Ukraine is due to be widely discussed.

Russian strikes on Ukraine overnight into Tuesday killed four people, Ukrainian officials said, while also cutting the electricity supply to thousands.

The strikes took place in the cities Dnipro, Kryvyi Rih and Pavlohrad in the southeastern region of Dnipropetrovsk, regional governor Oleksandr Hanzha said on Telegram. The barrage included anti-ship and ballistic missiles, four cruise missiles and 212 drones.

The region of Dnipropetrovsk is the country's industrial heartland, where major production industries are located, including steel-making and machine building.

In the city of Dnipro, four people were killed and six were injured. According to Hanzha, the strike also damaged a local business and a warehouse.

Ukraine strikes Russian oil refinery; 1 killed

In Russia, Ukrainian drones killed one person and injured four in the Samara region, local authorities said. The region is home to important facilities, including oil refineries.

Moscow's Defense Ministry said it had intercepted 297 drones over various regions in Russia overnight.

Samara is located some 1,000 kilometers southeast of Russian capital Moscow.

Zelenskyy attends UN General Assembly

Russia and Ukraine have both stepped up attacks recently, as the war has dragged on for four and a half years with no end in sight.

Both parties deny targeting civilians, while also blaming each other for civilian casualties.

The latest attacks come as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is planning to meet US counterpart Donald Trump in New York on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly. Russian President Vladimir Putin is not expected at the UN General Assembly.

Edited by: Rana Taha

entries.title: Male infertility is 'grossly underreported'
entries.summary: It's not all on women anymore — doctors do test men for sperm count and motility. But still too few men get checked, possibly due to a misconception that a healthy sex life means healthy sperm. Spoiler: It doesn't.
entries.content:
ScienceGlobal issues

Male infertility: 'Grossly underreported' and misunderstood

September 22, 2026

It's not all on women anymore — doctors do test men for sperm count and motility. But still too few men get checked, possibly due to a misconception that a healthy sex life means healthy sperm. Spoiler: It doesn't.

Sperm counts have fallen globally by more than 51% since 1973, and the decline is accelerating. That's according to a 2026 review of studies published in the journal Antioxidants. But men are less likely to get tested than women for infertility.

"Male infertility is understated. It is so huge a problem," said Edidiong Akang, a reproductive biologist at the University of Lagos, Nigeria.

In a study led by Akang and published in the journal Scientific Reports in 2023, he and his colleagues analyzed semen samples from more than 17,000 men and found that the quality of sperm shape and size (known as sperm morphology) had deteriorated by about 50% between 2010 and 2019.

Sperm motility (how well it swims to the female egg) had also dropped significantly — in Nigeria, for example, by 87% in that same period.

And yet, as Akang told DW, the male share of infertility is "grossly underreported" and, as a result, misunderstood.

What affects a man's fertility?

Male fertility depends on a healthy sperm shape, size, motility, and its concentration and count. The latter is often used as an indication of male fertility because many millions try to reach the egg but only one or few make it. They need to be strong swimmers.

These factors depend on other, underlying health conditions: Male infertility can be caused by weight gain, stress, poor sleep, smoking, microplastics and cannabis use.

Weight gain in particular effects the testes (also: testicles), which produce sperm and hormones like testosterone.

The testes function best at two degrees centigrade cooler than the rest of the body. Fat raises the temperature, and that can affect the sperm — its concentration, count and motility.

Why male infertility often goes undiagnosed

Male sexual health is often overlooked, possibly because men under the age of 40 don't generally have a regular reason to get checked — if you're older than 40, you may get your prostate checked annually. But even a urologist won't check your sperm count unless you ask them.

Women, on the other hand, get a monthly signal — their menstrual cycle — and may be able to infer from that that something is wrong.

A man gets no such natural signals about his fertility until he tries to conceive with a woman. And by then he may be 30 or 40, when some health outcomes are hard to reverse.

Riffat Bibi, a clinical embryologist who has led an IVF laboratory in Pakistan for 17 years, described what men often say on arrival: "Okay, check my wife first."

Sometimes a mother-in-law brings the daughter-in-law, which also suggests that the mother-in-law thinks: It can't be my son's fault.

And some patients "feel sexual activity is equivalent to fertility, which it is not," said Bibi.

Roughly 80% of Bibi's cases now involve a male factor, far above the 50-50 split long assumed, and her laboratory has had to adapt, she said.

They are also seeing this development in IVF (in vitro fertilization) treatment. Sperm has become so poor that nearly all her clients need an embryologist to pick a single sperm and inject it directly into the egg.

But there is another factor than many men don't talk about much: synthetic testosterone — or steroids.

Testosterone shuts down sperm production

Some men, keen on a muscley body, suppress their own sperm production unknowingly by taking anabolic steroids, a synthetic form of testosterone.

The appeal of anabolic steroids is straightforward, said Harrison Pope, a Harvard Medical School researcher: Steroids enhance athletic performance. A steroid user, who drinks, smokes and skips half of his workouts can outperform a dedicated, clean athlete.

Pope, who has studied steroids for three decades, said "they are highly effective."

But what you gain in athletic performance, you lose in fertility, because an over-supply of testosterone can shut down sperm production.

A healthy body will keep testosterone levels in balance. Too little testosterone can also impede sperm production.

Sperm production can restart if you stop taking testosterone supplements, but Pope said it depends on your age, and much you were taking and for how long.

Occasional steroid users usually regain a "normal" sperm count. The World Health Organization considers a normal sperm count to be about 16 million sperm per milliliter of semen (or higher).

Heavy, long-term steroid users, meanwhile, often do not recover or return to normal sperm production.

Users typically take steroids in cycles – weeks on the drug, followed by a a break to let the body recover. But when Dutch researchers followed 100 men through one cycle of steroids and for a year after, they found two-thirds still had very low sperm counts, some had no sperm at all, and a year later, their counts had still not returned to normal.

Not everyone takes steroids, and yet falling sperm counts still occur. Take India, for example, where Chirag Bhandari, runs the Institute of Andrology and Sexual Health in Jaipur. Bhandari estimates that steroids account for less than 0.1% of the country's falling sperm counts. Overweight, heat-stress and smoking are usually the cause.

If a man is tested early, his sperm count will often return to normal within six to twelve months, both Bhandari and Bibi said. But the longer the problem goes undetected, the less likely that becomes.

Edited by: Zulfikar Abbany

entries.title: UNGA: Leaders gather as General Assembly kicks off
entries.summary: World leaders have begun gathering in New York for the UN General Assembly. US President Trump will address the body on Tuesday, as will his Finnish, French and Turkish counterparts. Follow DW for the latest.
entries.content:
Published September 22, 2026last updated September 22, 2026

World leaders have begun gathering in New York for the UN General Assembly. US President Trump will address the body on Tuesday, as will his Finnish, French and Turkish counterparts. Follow DW for the latest.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres will officially open the world body's 81st General Assembly — which runs through next Monday — at its New York Headquarters on Tuesday
  • US President Donald Trump will feature among Tuesday's speakers, with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and French President Emmanuel Macron also speaking throughout the day
  • Trump is expected to address the war he launched against Tehran and the fall out it has brought for the global economy
  • The General Assembly comes at a time of global uncertainty as global conflict, environmental crisis and massive technical disruption foist uncertainty upon the global population

Read below for all the top headlines, videos and analyses on the 81 UN General Assembly from Sept 22, to Sept 28, 2026:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section World leaders gather in New York for 81st UNGA session

World leaders gather in New York for 81st UNGA session

United Nations Secretary General Antonio Guterres and Assembly President Khalilur Rahman

will open the UN's 81st General Assembly (UNGA) in New York on Tuesday morning as world leaders gather for their annual six-day confab.

As Guterres puts it, "In a world marked by turbulence, division and uncertainty, the United Nations is more necessary than ever."

This year's session comes as war — mainly in Ukraine and Iran — climate catastrophe, and the specter of artificial intelligence overshadow the world's myriad other problems.

The session offers an opportunity for leaders to politick in person with numerous bilateral meetings expected to take place on the main stage's sidelines.

The event will likely get off to a rousing start when US President Donald Trump — who has delivered belligerent and fantastical addresses in the past — takes the stage after Brazilian President Inacio Lula Da Silva in the morning session and before Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan.   

Further speakers will include leaders from Africa, Central Asia, Europe, Scandinavia, South America and the Middle East.

A full schedule is available here

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Good morning and welcome to our coverage of the 81st United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) in New York. 

The day's schedule includes an opening address from UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres that comes at a time when the body itself is under threat from US President Donald Trump — who has repeatedly expressed his willingness to renege on US financial obligations to the body if it does not bend to his will — and in the face of myriad global crises ranging from financial and environmental disasters to spreading conflict, rampant disease and the looming threat of so-called artificial intelligence.

Among those who will join Guterres and Trump are Turkish leader Recep Tayyip Erdogan, as well as the leaders of Finland and Lithuania, and France's President Emmanuel Macron.

Stay tuned to DW for the latest during the confab, which ends next Monday, September 28.

entries.title: 'Swan Song': New book by Princess Diana's brother drops
entries.summary: A memoir penned by Charles Spencer on his older sister's life has been released, opening old royal wounds nearly three decades after Princess Diana's death.
entries.content:
United Kingdom

'Swan Song': New book by Princess Diana's brother drops

September 22, 2026

A memoir penned by Charles Spencer on his older sister's life has been released, opening old royal wounds nearly three decades after Princess Diana's death.

Charles Spencer's book about his late sister Princess Diana's life and former marriage to Britain's now King Charles III hit bookstores on Tuesday.

The book titled "Swan Song: Diana, My Sister" is being published globally by Penguin and has been translated into 12 languages.

The memoir triggered a royal row even before it went on sale, after some of its pre-published extracts —  laden with Spencer's explosive claims  —  received a rare reaction and rebuttal from the king.

Charles Spencer, the 9th Earl Spencer, is Diana's younger brother and has long clashed with the royal House of Windsor over how they treated the princess.

What does Charles Spencer say in his memoir of Princess Diana?

In one of the claims that made a splash ahead the new book's release, Spencer accused Charles of sounding "giddily elated" and "like a lottery winner" when he had called him after Diana's death.

Spencer also writes that he had argued against plans for Charles and Diana's sons, William and Harry, to walk in their mother's funeral procession in 1997, saying that she would not have wanted them to go through that ordeal.

Spencer claims Charles "went ballistic" during the argument , telling him: "Rest assured, we'll forget her soon enough."

William was 15-years-old at the time and Harry was 12.

The world was moved by somber visuals of the young princes walking behind Diana's coffin.

How has King Charles III reacted to Spencer's claims?

Following the release of the book's excerpts last week, Buckingham Palace published a strongly-worded statement.

"His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgement and color memory in ways others do not recognize, even many years after such a loss," it said in a statement considered rare as far as responses from the royal household go.

Princess Diana's life and death

In 1981, a 20-year-old Lady Diana Spencer married a 32-year-old Charles, who was then the Prince of Wales, in a fairytale wedding that was televised globally.

Their whirlwind romance soon hit rock bottom and culminated in a public breakdown of their marriage. Diana famously told the BBC in an interview that "there were three of us in this marriage, so it was a bit crowded" in reference to Charles' ⁠relationship with Camilla Parker ​Bowles.

Diana, known as the people's princess, was loved by people from all over the world. Her popularity led to her experiencing a media frenzy that lasted nearly all her adult life.

The royal couple divorced in 1996 and Diana died a year later, aged 36, in a car crash in Paris as she was being pursued by paparazzi.

Charles married Parker Bowles in 2005.

Edited by: Rana Taha

entries.title: Will Germany have enough gas this winter?
entries.summary: Germany's gas storage sites are far less full than in recent years. Officials say supplies are secure, but analysts warn that a cold winter or import disruptions could push prices higher. So how secure is the supply?
entries.content:
September 22, 2026

Germany's gas storage sites are far less full than in recent years. Officials say supplies are secure, but analysts warn that a cold winter or import disruptions could push prices higher. So how secure is the supply?

As of mid-September 2026, Germany had stored just about 141 terawatt-hours of gas, accounting for around 57% of the country's total storage capacity.  

Last winter just under 134 terawatt-hours of gas were withdrawn from storage, according to the Federal Network Agency, the agency that monitors the country's electricity and gas networks.

At first glance, the numbers sounds reassuring, especially since last winter was quite cold and therefore required a lot of heating. But compared to previous years, natural gas storage levels are low.

On September 4, Markus Söder, the premier of Bavaria, called for intervention by the federal government.

A few days later, the opposition Green Party accused the economy minister of negligence. "The gas storage facilities are not full. We are facing a potential shortage," said Britta Hasselmann, co-leader of the Greens' parliamentary group.

Such statements have raised concerns about potential gas shortages in Germany this winter.

To assess the current situation, however, various factors such as imports and the diversification of supply sources need to be taken into account , not least since Germany is no longer as dependent on a single importer as it was on Russia until 2022.

Will Germany have enough gas?

Most experts interviewed by DW are not concerned about the winter gas supply.

Charlie Grüneberg, spokesperson for the German Gas and Hydrogen Industry association, points to the contracts that have been signed for the medium term. "Anyone who has contractually secured their gas needs for the winter with a reliable supplier will receive the agreed quantities," he said.

Sebastian Heinermann, managing director of INES, a German association for gas and hydrogen storage system operators, is more cautious.

He pointed out that it's technically possible to fill gas storage facilities in Germany to around 77%, but this would require filling at a level that "has not been observed even once in the past three weeks," Heinermann said. "If this trend continues unchanged, the fill level will reach only about 65% by November 1."

Still, the Federal Network Agency sees no cause for concern.

"The gas supply in Germany is stable," the agency's spokesperson, Nadia Affani, told DW. "Security of supply is currently guaranteed. Based on the latest information, the Federal Network Agency continues to assess the risk of a gas supply crunch as low."

Germany's Ministry for Economic Affairs and Energy shared a similar assessment. The ministry "is monitoring all developments very closely to ensure security of supply. There are currently no signs of a supply shortage," said spokesperson Susanne Ungrad.

Officials downplay supply risks

She also pointed to an array of factors that determine the price of natural gas like available storage, ongoing imports via pipelines and LNG terminals, demand and the situation on the international energy markets.

"We are prepared for further developments," Ungrad stressed.

Grüneberg also takes a more holistic view.

"The key factor is whether enough gas can be procured and transported to and through Germany. Supply contracts, storage facilities, pipeline imports and LNG are all interlinked," he underscored.

"Thanks to investments in LNG terminals, new import routes and reverse-flow capabilities, the infrastructure is now significantly more robust than it was in 2022."

Gas prices rise ahead of winter

As the winter approaches and people start heating their homes more, gas prices tend to climb. This trend is already evident, said Heinermann.

"In the second quarter, the gas price across various contracts on the futures market stood at around €46 ($52) per megawatt-hour. Recently, the gas price has risen to over €80."

Olaf Geyer from the US consulting firm Arthur D. Little, who has been monitoring the German market, said there is no immediate supply problem, but: "If the winter turns out to be cold or there are disruptions on the import side, prices could rise quickly."

Grüneberg said "reliable price forecasts" are difficult to make and noted that low storage levels could cause prices to rise "if additional volumes have to be procured on the market."

However, there are no signs of a shortage on the supply side. "As things stand today, there are no indications of a physical shortage of supply by the end of winter. The futures markets are not signaling this at the moment either," said Grüneberg.

The German economy ministry points out that "the prices currently quoted for forward contracts for the winter are only slightly higher than the spot market prices for immediate transactions."

"The usual summer-winter spread, which made it economically viable to store gas during the summer months, was therefore not present," it added.

The "spread" is based on the principle of buying gas cheaply in summer and selling it at higher prices in winter. This year, gas prices rose following the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, undermining that seasonal pattern.

How to refill storage faster

Geyer, who also focuses on the summer-winter spread, said storage facilities aren't fuller this time round because it hasn't been economically viable.

"For the future, we need better incentives for filling storage facilities — and risk management on the part of utilities that looks not only at the purchase price but also at how much actual consumption can deviate from projections," he underlined.

Heinermann also called for effective economic incentives to fill gas storage facilities.

"In the medium term, Germany needs a reliable market framework that, through incentives, obligations or a combination of both, ensures sufficient storage levels on a long-term basis while preserving as much market-based flexibility as possible."

This article was originally written in German.

entries.title: Germany news: VW to step up cost-cutting program
entries.summary: Volkswagen's chief says the carmaker will accelerate its streamlining measures as workers protest. The Israeli ambassador says the Left Party win in Berlin polls poses a risk to the city's Jewish community. DW has more.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany news: VW to step up cost-cutting program

Published September 22, 2026last updated September 22, 2026

Volkswagen's chief says the carmaker will accelerate its streamlining measures as workers protest. The Israeli ambassador says the Left Party win in Berlin polls poses a risk to the city's Jewish community. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • The brand chief at carmaker Volkswagen says 'there is no time to lose' as the company pursues a drastic cost-cutting agenda
  • Israel's ambassador to Germany says the victory of the Left Party in Berlin state elections poses 'a concrete and direct danger' to the capital's Jewish population
  • The conservative bloc of Friedrich Merz is marking 150 years since the birth of the Federal Republic's first chancellor, Konrad Adenauer, with a conference
  • A worker at a ride at the Oktoberfest in Munich has died from injuries sustained in an accident, police say

This is a roundup of the top headlines from and about Germany on Tuesday, September 22, 2026:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.

Skip next section IN DEPTH: Tough times for Merz after election debacles

IN DEPTH: Tough times for Merz after election debacles

Chancellor Friedrich Merz has been forced to reassess his Christian Democratic Union's (CDU's) political direction after the party suffered large losses in two recent elections, even failing to gain a seat in one state parliament.

Many in Germany are questioning whether he can remain in power, though he himself has remained defiant.

DW's Marcel Fürstenau has this analysis of the fallout from Sunday's elections in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and Berlin: Germany: Chancellor Merz braces for difficult days ahead

Skip next section German electronics exports surge in 2026

German electronics exports surge in 2026

A total of €23.5 billion ($26.8 billion) of German electronics goods were exported in July, an increase of 11.9% year-on-year, an industry group said on Tuesday.

That is a slight rise on the already strong growth seen up to the end of June, according to Andreas Gontermann, chief economist at the German Electro and Digital Industry Association (ZVEI).

Over the first seven months of the year, German electronics were exported to the tune of €162.9 billion, a rise of 9.7% compared with the same period last year.

Most of the growth came with exports to EU countries, which made up 90% of the increase and rose 17% in the first seven months above the level in the same period a year ago.

But German firms also exported electronics worth €2.7 billion to the United States in July, an increase of 23.3% year-on-year despite the new tariffs imposed by the Trump administration.

However, exports to China continued to decline, dropping by 10.8% to €1.8 billion.

Skip next section Worker dies in accident at Oktoberfest

Worker dies in accident at Oktoberfest

A worker at Munich's Oktoberfest has died of serious injuries suffered in an accident at a drop tower, where people are carried high into the air in a gondola that then drops rapidly, police said early on Tuesday.

They said the worker appeared to have been in an area where he was not meant to be and was then struck and possibly crushed.

The 52-year-old man was resuscitated at the scene and taken to hospital with life-threatening injuries, but later died.

No one using the ride was ever in danger, police said.

Witnesses of the accident have received support from a crisis intervention team.

Skip next section Number of accidents on way to school rose in 2025

Number of accidents on way to school rose in 2025

There were almost 90,700 accidents involving pupils on their way to school last year, a rise of 3.8%, according to statistics from the German Social Accident Insurance Institutions (DGUV).

Of those accidents, 25 had a fatal outcome, compared with 15 in 2024, the DGUV said.

Accidents at the schools themselves also rose by 2%, with 1,032,500 cases registered, five of them fatal.

In a survey carried out last year by the Forsa polling institute for the DGUV, a third of the participating parents said their child had experienced at least one dangerous situation on the way to school.

They saw the biggest dangers amid a lack of continuous bike paths and crossing roads with heavy traffic.

Skip next section Israeli ambassador sees Left Party victory in Berlin as danger to Jews

Israeli ambassador sees Left Party victory in Berlin as danger to Jews

The Israeli ambassador to Germany, Ron Prosor, says the win by the socialist Left Party at Berlin state elections on Sunday poses a "direct existential danger" for the Jewish community in the German capital.

"The strong performance of the Left at the Berlin elections should worry anyone who cherishes the continued existence of Jewish life in this city," he told the German DPA news agency.

"The completely unbridled antisemitism that has manifested itself in this party has been given a new political dimension by its rise to the strongest force," Prosor said.

Elif Eralp, the Left's top candidate who might become the governing mayor of Berlin, has said that antisemitism was not stronger in her party than in society at large.

"The overwhelming majority of the party is clearly in favor of protecting Jewish life and the strength of Jewish life," she said at a discussion run by the Jewish Community in Berlin (JGzB).

"Antisemitism is a problem in society in general and exists also within the Left Party," she said.

Skip next section Volkswagen brand chief pledges to step on the gas with cost-cutting measures

Volkswagen brand chief pledges to step on the gas with cost-cutting measures

German carmaker Volkswagen intends to accelerate the ongoing cost-cutting program at its core brand, Thomas Schäfer, the brand chief of Volkswagen Passenger Cars said on Monday.

"We have absolutely no time to lose and will therefore significantly ramp up our performance program once again," Schäfer said.

His remarks at a staff meeting at the company's main plant in Wolfsburg came as automotive workers across Germany held protests, calling on management to secure jobs.

Schäfer said around 16,300 redundancies have been finalized in Germany, with a total of just under 28,800 agreed upon by 2030, close to the target of 35,000.

He called this "good progress," but warned that it was not enough.

In early September, Volkswagen said it would be cutting a total of 100,000 jobs worldwide by the end of the decade.

Germany's carmakers are under pressure from increasing Chinese competition, while also having to contend with high energy prices, US tariffs and falling demand at home.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Guten Tag from DW's newsroom in Bonn!

Fallout from the weekend's state elections continues to dominate headlines in Germany, and we will be looking at party reactions to the results, which represent a considerable upheaval in the country's political landscape.

Germany's automotive industry is also facing great changes in the face of multiple challenges, with key carmaker Volkswagen doubling down on streamlining measures it says are needed to remain competitive.

And, as a reflection of the security challenges currently facing Europe, the Ruhr city of Essen is hosting a new defense industry trade fair, Eudex, featuring 350 exhibitors from 28 countries.

Read on here for more details on these and other stories currently hitting the headlines in Germany.

entries.title: Germany: Chancellor Merz braces for difficult days ahead
entries.summary: Germany's far-right AfD and the socialist Left Party gained ground in recent state elections, while the centrist parties lost support. The biggest loser is Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany: Chancellor Merz braces for difficult days ahead

September 22, 2026

Germany's far-right AfD and the socialist Left Party gained ground in recent state elections, while the centrist parties lost support. The biggest loser is Chancellor Friedrich Merz.

Why have the results of the two German state elections held on Sunday, September 20, thrown the spotlight on the federal government led by the Christian Democrats (CDU) and its chancellor Friedrich Merz?

For the first time, the party failed to reach the required 5% of votes to enter parliament in the northeastern coastal state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. It marks the first time in its history that the CDU has failed to enter a state parliament. In the city-state of Berlin, where the CDU was incumbent, the party suffered heavy losses and is likely to end up on the opposition benches.

The chancellor says he is aware of the significance. "This election is a profound turning point. It is a dramatic and unprecedented result for the CDU in Germany that we could not clear the 5% threshold. For an entire bloc to leave the state parliament is a heavy blow, and that will resonate with us for a long time to come," he said.

At the same time, Merz conceded that federal policy, which had failed to convince the public, had played a role in the defeats. Most voters are also not satisfied with the chancellor himself. However, he also sees another cause: "We are experiencing a dramatic shift of the party-political system in Germany, as are many other countries," Merz said.

The chancellor pointed to the competition at the political margins: "In [Sunday's] elections, more than 40% of the vote went to forces which are destructive, which question our political, parliamentary system. And who attempt to excite people with radical and simple solutions," was his analysis. Merz did not name the parties he was referring to, but he clearly meant the Alternative for Germany (AfD) and the Left Party. 

The AfD is classified as "confirmed right-wing extremist" by the Office for the Protection of the Constitution, Germany's domestic intelligence agency, in five of Germany's 16 federal states — but not in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, both regions in which it was able to significantly grow its share of the vote.

In the German capital, the AfD's result grew from 9% to 16% compared to the previous election. In the northeastern coastal state, the party more than doubled its result, to 38%. AfD co-leader Tino Chrupalla said, alluding to his party's color: "The blue wave cannot be stopped." 

Criticism of the CDU's 'firewall' policy

The AfD's other co-leader Alice Weidel, concluded that the CDU had been pulverized and that the chancellor's resignation is "overdue." "This clearly shows that we have replaced the CDU as the party of the masses," she said. 

"That is also the result of a very unintelligent firewall policy," Weidel added, referring to the CDU's so-called resolution of incompatibility, which rejects coalitions with both her party and the socialist Left.

The AfD's claim to have taken the place of the CDU is unfounded, according to political scientist Wolfgang Muno from the University of Rostock in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. The AfD is no big tent party representing conservative interests, he told DW: "It is a right-wing extremist party which has managed to bring together various groups."

Muno's opinion of the Left Party is vastly different to Merz's: "We have seen that the Left has really moved toward being a pragmatic, democratically oriented party. Therefore, there is no reason for the Christian Democrats to simply accuse them of being extremists, because the Left is not an extremist party," Muno said.

The Left Party faces antisemitism allegations

Muno considers criticism of Israeli policies legitimate. At the same time, he notes that it had been accompanied by antisemitic incidents . He expects the Left to send a clear signal that such things are not acceptable. "But not being open to cooperating with a democratic Left Party is, in my opinion, a bad sign," he said, referring to the CDU. 

In Berlin, the socialist Left with lead candidate Elif Eralp succeeded in doubling its previous result to 26% and won an election in the city-state for the first time. A scandalous campaign event appearance by rapper Dahabflex, who sang about wishing death for Israel's soldiers, appears not to have damaged the party. Its district association in Neukölln, which had invited the singer, said it intended to clarify the matter.

Josef Schuster, President of the Central Council of Jews in Germany, is skeptical: "So far there have been no personnel or political consequences." He appealed to the Social Democrats and Greens not to form a coalition with the Berlin election winners.

Federal co-leader of the Left, Ines Schwerdtner, told DW that she would not tolerate antisemitism among the party's ranks. "We are there in Berlin to build bridges — Elif Eralp is doing that. And within the party we will absolutely ensure that something like this does not happen."

Eralp, whose parents fled to Germany after a military coup in Turkey, could become the first mayor from the Left in Berlin. About 200,000 of the German capital's four million residents have Turkish roots.

Against this background, the lead candidate considers her and her party's success as an important sign: "I view this election result also as a victory for solidarity, for diversity, for democracy, against the shift to the right which we are experiencing in many places in this country," she said.

Merz vows to push through with welfare reforms

Manuela Schwesig, the Social Democrats' (SPD) lead candidate in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, scored a partial success. With about 36% of the vote, her party came in just behind the AfD, but she has good prospects of being able to remain state premier: "I will propose to my party that we hold talks with both the Greens and the Left — the two democratic parties represented in the state parliament — and fulfil our electoral mandate," she said.

The incumbent, who has held the office since 2017, is critical of Chancellor Friedrich Merz's announcement that he wants to press on with his course of deep cuts to the welfare system. The most controversial is the planned pension reform. "He is misjudging the situation of what the people on the ground think, at least in my state," Schwesig said.

She reminded Merz of the agreement his party made with the SPD at the federal level: "I would like for the coalition to implement exactly what we negotiated together in the coalition agreement, namely that the pension without deductions remains possible after 45 years of contribution."

This agreement is currently hanging in the balance. Like the SPD's Schwesig, some eastern German CDU state premiers have spoken out against the chancellor's plans.

Despite this, the SPD faces a dilemma because at the federal level it is part of the government with the CDU. The party's co-leader, Bärbel Bas , now wants to draw the "correct conclusions" from the results of the state parliament elections.

However, she also said that the party had taken responsibility in the federal government. "We are in this coalition, and we also want to maintain it. Nevertheless, we must also accept the analysis from the campaign trail that the people are not satisfied with the upcoming reforms. That means that we, together with our coalition partner, must seek solutions."

This article was translated from German.

entries.title: Princess Diana's brother makes explosive claims on royals in new memoir
entries.summary: Here are some of the key revelations from Charles Earl Spencer's highly anticipated memoir "Swan Song: Diana, My Sister." It has already provoked Buckingham Palace to react.
entries.content:
September 22, 2026

Here are some of the key revelations from Charles Earl Spencer's highly anticipated memoir "Swan Song: Diana, My Sister." It has already provoked Buckingham Palace to react.

In the new book "Swan Song: Diana, My Sister," Charles Spencer, the 9th Earl Spencer, offers his perspective on the life of his late sister, Diana, Princess of Wales.

As British tabloid culture ensures that every feud and controversy linked to the royal family gets amplified into a major public debate, the memoir started making headlines before its publication on September 22.

Among some of the key revelations of the book, he says that he believes that Diana had ADHD, and that "as part of that condition she suffered from Rejection Sensitive Dysphoria," which he describes as "an intense emotional pain in the face of others' rejection or criticism."

Spencer also claims their father developed a "romantic connection" with the future Queen Elizabeth II, until he was warned off her by Lord Mountbatten, who was the maternal uncle and close mentor of the queen's husband, Prince Philip.

But most polemically, Spencer revisits one of the British royal family's most painful chapters: the aftermath of Diana's tragic death in a car crash on August 31, 1997.

'We'll forget her soon enough'

Spencer writes that when Queen Elizabeth II first heard of Diana's accident, her initial reaction was: "What is she up to now?" before the gravity of the situation became clear.

Diana's death sparked a global outpouring of grief. In the aftermath of the car crash, the royals faced strong public backlash for their delayed and cold response to the tragedy. The Queen's first public address came five days after Diana's death.

In his book, Spencer suggests that some inside Buckingham Palace were "relieved — indeed pleased" that she had died. He also recounts a phone conversation with King Charles, then-Prince of Wales that happened days after her death. According to Spencer, the prince sounded "giddily elated — like a lottery winner."

Spencer writes that they discussed how he objected to having Prince William, then 15, and Prince Harry, then 12, walk behind their mother's coffin during the funeral procession at the internationally televised funeral.

Spencer felt it would be traumatic to put the boys in the media spotlight just after their mother had died. He writes in the book that he believes the boys were used as a protective shield for Charles, as Buckingham Palace officials feared "members of the public might shout abuse at him," whereas the children's presence "would surely guarantee against insults flying."

Spencer also recounts Diana's belief that Prince Charles had already become jealous of her popularity decades earlier.

He describes how Prince Charles went into a "stream of anger" during the phone conversation after her death. The princess's brother writes that her former husband unleashed "his pent-up contempt for Diana, and his horror that the world was so bowled over by her death. 'Rest assured,' he hissed, 'we'll forget her soon enough!'"

But nearly 30 years after the fatal car crash, Diana remains a global icon. The 36-year-old was a glamorous celebrity, renowned for her advocacy for different causes, including her groundbreaking support for AIDS patients.

Buckingham Palace directly reacted to the first excerpt published in the Daily Mail: "While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle. His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and color memory in ways others do not recognize, even many years after such a loss."

In contrast, the Palace met Prince Harry's accusations in his 2023 memoir "Spare" with total institutional silence, applying the royals' traditional public relations strategy of "Never complain, never explain."

Speaking on behalf of the 'blood family'

The feud between Earl Spencer and Buckingham Palace is not new.

Spencer famously delivered a passionate eulogy for his sister at Westminster Abbey in 1997. In it, he not only criticized the role of the paparazzi in the accident, calling his sister the "most hunted person of the modern age," but also set himself apart from the royals by referring to his blood ties with Diana in a promise to protect her boys "from a similar fate."

"I pledge that we, your blood family, will do all we can to continue the imaginative way in which you were steering these two exceptional young men so that their souls are not simply immersed by duty and tradition but can sing openly as you planned," he said at the time.

On the day of the funeral, Spencer writes, Queen Elizabeth II offered through intermediaries to posthumously restore Diana's "Her Royal Highness" (HRH) title. Spencer declined, as he felt the gesture had little meaning after her death.

Even though Buckingham Palace has always insisted Diana gave up the title voluntarily, Spencer writes that she was left "dreadfully hurt" by its removal amid her divorce with Charles.

Intrusive tabloid culture led to her death

In his book, Spencer returns to the themes he addressed in his eulogy, accusing the editors and publishers who bought intrusive photos of Diana of having contributed to killing his sister.

According to him, British tabloid culture turned into system that profited from Diana's suffering and encouraged increasingly extreme invasions of privacy.

After the divorce, large sections of the media began portraying Diana as unstable, manipulative, difficult or attention-seeking. Paparazzi would provoke distress and photograph her reaction; newspapers would then publish stories suggesting she was unstable.

She was unable to escape media scrutiny, making her extremely unhappy: "It is a sad fact that, in her later years, Diana drove herself more than once to Beachy Head, the highest chalk sea cliff in England, while contemplating ending it all," Spencer writes, adding: "Her love for her sons stopped her from going further."

A lucrative release ahead of 30th anniversary of Diana's death

While Spencer has long criticized the destructive nature of the British tabloid system, the promotion of his memoir relies on the exact ecosystem he decries. He has sold serialization rights of the book to the UK's Daily Mail — one of the very tabloid outlets frequently associated with intense royal scrutiny.

Some critics accuse him of wanting to cash in on the tragedy, with the high-profile book published just ahead of the 30th anniversary of Diana's death.

His supporters however feel that Diana's brother is justified to share his personal perspective on their shared experience, noting that many other authors have profited off her legacy over the decades.

Spencer has stated that his account aims to correct decades of "untruths that have become accepted over time" and inaccurate portrayals of his late sister by outside biographers and commentators over the years.

"At heart, this is a brother's simple tribute to an extraordinary sister," Earl Spencer wrote of his own work on Instagram, adding, "A month ago I read 'Swan Song' out, over three days, for a recording so that it could be available on audiobook. When I finished the recording, I thought: 'That is exactly what I wanted and needed to say — and she would, I reckon, have approved of every word.'"

Edited by: Brenda Haas

entries.title: India news: Police investigate alleged gang-rape in Delhi
entries.summary: While India is fuming over a viral video of two minors being harassed in Bihar, a case of an alleged gang-rape of a minor has emerged in a posh Delhi neighborhood. Meanwhile, India's foreign minister is at the UNGA.
entries.content:
Published September 22, 2026last updated September 22, 2026

While India is fuming over a viral video of two minors being harassed in Bihar, a case of an alleged gang-rape of a minor has emerged in a posh Delhi neighborhood. Meanwhile, India's foreign minister is at the UNGA.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Delhi police look into report regarding a minor who was allegedly gang-raped in New Delhi
  • Indian Foreign Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar urges multilateralism at UNGA in New York

Here's a roundup of the headlines from India on Tuesday, September 22: 

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section Modi lauds Indian women's cricket team for gold win

Modi lauds Indian women's cricket team for gold win

Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Tuesday congratulated the Indian women's cricket team for cinching the gold medal at the Asian Games in Japan. 

"A splendid triumph for Indian cricket!" the Prime Minister's Office wrote in a post on X quoting Modi. "It was a commanding performance at the Games, marked by confidence, skill and wonderful teamwork...The team has made the nation proud and will inspire countless young cricketers across the country," he said.

The prime minister also congratulated athlete Suchika Tariyal on winning a bronze in mixed martial arts and securing "India’s first-ever Asian Games medal in this field".

"Her achievement is especially significant, highlighting her dedication and zeal," the prime minister's office wrote in a separate post.

Skip next section IN DEPTH — India's road rage: When cars become weapons

IN DEPTH — India's road rage: When cars become weapons

A road altercation in Gurugram, a suburb of New Delhi, went viral last week after a 27-year-old female biker was allegedly chased and hit by a car. The case was only the latest example of how quickly a dispute on India's increasingly crowded roads can turn violent.

India's roads are notoriously dangerous, with government figures showing 485 people were killed in crashes on an average day in 2024. The data also indicates that the number of vehicles is currently growing much faster than the expansion of the road network.

Notably, SUVs accounted for about 2.63 million vehicles, or 56% of India's car sales, in the 12 months leading up to March 2026, according to industry data. While more SUVs on the road does not necessarily mean more aggressive driving, the vehicles' size, height and presence can change the dynamics of a confrontation.

"For some drivers it is an expression of strength and domination," former police officer Yashovardhan Azad told DW.

Read the full report here.

Skip next section Asian Games: Women's cricket team scores first gold of the season

Asian Games: Women's cricket team scores first gold of the season

The Indian women's cricket team has won the nation its first Gold medal at the 2026 Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, after scoring the highest women's total in the event's history. 

The team scored 216-3 with 18 fours and 13 sixes, defeating Sri Lanka for its second consecutive gold at the Asian Games.

Team captain Harmanpreet Kaur won the toss and opted to bat first, unleashing Shafali Verma and Smriti Mandhana as the opening pair. Mandhana's 79 runs undoubtedly helped cement India's victory.

At the same time, the Indian men's cricket team had a surprisingly close call with Japan.

The T20 World Champions narrowly survived an upset, edging out Japan by just two runs in a rain-shortened T20 match. This was the first-ever T20 international match between the teams, celebrating 75 years of diplomatic relations at Japan's Sano International Cricket Ground outside Tokyo.

Japan is ranked 41st by the International Cricket Council.

This match, however, was not part of the Asian Games. Japan will play the opening match of the men's T20 cricket at the event against Afghanistan on Thursday.

Skip next section Hanuman statue in Texas becomes talking point ahead of midterm elections

Hanuman statue in Texas becomes talking point ahead of midterm elections

A massive 90-foot statue of Hindu deity Hanuman, in Texas, has become a political talking point ahead of the US midterm elections, after a conservative YouTuber called for its removal. 

Named the 'Statue of the Union', the idol has been a controversial figure since it was erected in Sugarland, Texas in 2024. It has come back into focus after YouTuber and MAGA supporter Jesse Hughes brought it up on social media platform X.

“Btw, when we win, we are tearing this down,” YouTuber Jesse Hughes said, sharing a photograph of the statue. His comment sparked a backlash among Indian Americans, especially Hindus.

The Coalition of Hindus of North America expressed its "horror at the open religious bigotry being mainstreamed," after it was asked by an X user to respond to Hughes' statement.

"American Hindus are under attack as never before and we need to remember that it is upon each one of us to stand up and speak up against religious bigotry and Hinduphobia," it said.

About 570,000 Indians resided in the state of Texas as of 2023, according to Pew Research.

Skip next section First Meta, now Google will report child abuse content directly to Indian authorities

First Meta, now Google will report child abuse content directly to Indian authorities

Tech giant Google on Monday said it has agreed to report content flagged as child sexual abuse material directly to Indian authorities.

Tech giants like Google and Meta, for years, have routed such reports through the US-based non-profit, National Center for Missing & Exploited Children.

Reuters had earlier reported that Indian government officials had pressed tech companies like Google and Microsoft to do so over concerns that the existing system delays reports and reaction time significantly.

Google "invests significantly ​to detect, deter, remove, and report child sexual abuse material," a spokesperson said, describing the move as part of the company's "ongoing discussions with the government of India."

Earlier this month, Meta also agreed to report child-safety related matters directly to law enforcement in India. 

The push for child safety on social media comes amid a global debate on imposing age restrictions on social media and tightening laws to protect children online. In July, an investigative report by the BBC found that Instagram had been running paid advertisements promoting child sexual abuse material in India.

India's Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) later ordered Instagram to disable all ads and content promoting and facilitating access to such material.

The ministry also demanded a detailed explanation on the issue and held several rounds of discussions with top Meta executives.

India is the largest market by users for both Meta and Google, giving the Indian government significant leverage to propose specific changes for the Indian market.

Skip next section Jaishankar urges multilateralism at UNGA

Jaishankar urges multilateralism at UNGA

India has co-sponsored an inaugural multilateralism summit on the sidelines of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly in New York "at a time when the global order is under stress," its top diplomat has said.

India's Foreign Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar said Delhi was glad to join the first ever Partners for Multilateralism, International Law, Peace & Prosperity (P4M) Summit held in the UN headquarters, the Press Trust of India reported.

The Indian foreign minister said that while the world has witnessed a steady rebalancing, "extreme competition, geopolitical tensions and actual conflicts have given this an entirely different character."

"If left unchecked, it would call into question the very spirit of international cooperation, and that is why it is so essential that multilateralism asserts itself strongly at this juncture," he said.

The summit was also co-sponsored by European Council President Antonio Costa, alongside countries including Kenya, Australia, Barbados, Brazil and Canada.

"We are at a critical moment for the world," Costa said. "Conflict is spreading, international law, including the United Nations Charter, is being repeatedly violated, including by permanent members of the United Nations Security Council, and the multilateral system is under stress."

Jaishankar's push for multilateralism comes when India is facing strained diplomatic ties with Washington under US President Donald Trump's second term. New Delhi's close relations with Russia and continued purchase of Russian oil has also been a point of strain with European counterparts. Several other countries are also forging new trade and security relations to diversify away from global powers like the US and China.

Skip next section Minor allegedly gang-raped in South Delhi neighborhood

Minor allegedly gang-raped in South Delhi neighborhood

A 17-year-old girl was allegedly gang-raped by three men posing as policemen in New Delhi on Monday evening, authorities said on Tuesday. 

The girl had been visiting a temple in southeast Delhi with a male friend, before they both retreated to a nearby park.

There, they were intercepted by three men who claimed to be police officers, authorities said, as reported by Hindustan Times. One of the accused is said to have held the male friend down while the girl was gang-raped. The men also reportedly threatened the duo with arrest if they reported the assault. The incident took place at about 7:30 p.m. local time (0200 GMT).

The Police received a call about the incident soon after and reached the spot, taking the girl for a medical examination. Authorities have launched a formal investigation under the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act (POCSO) and the Indian criminal law and teams were deployed to trace the accused.

One of the three accused of the gang-rape fired three shots at the police as they attempted to arrest him. During the exchange, one of the bullets struck an officer's bulletproof vest. The accused was shot in his right leg before he was arrested, news agency Press Trust of India reported.

The news of the Delhi gang-rape comes a day after a viral video from the eastern state of Bihar surfaced on social media, showing a group of about seven men molesting a minor girl while assaulting her male companion. The video has enraged netizens and political leaders alike.

Delhi remains one of the least safe cities for women in India, according to the National Annual Report and Index on Women's safety 2025.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage!

Welcome to our coverage!

Hello! and welcome to DW's India daily roundup.

This is Mahima Kapoor reporting from the New Delhi studio and I will be your guide through the biggest headlines of the day.

The Indian capital woke up to disturbing news of a minor who was allegedly gang-raped in an upscale Delhi neighborhood on Monday evening. The police were called in soon after, but the incident is yet another reminder of how Delhi remains one of the least safe cities in the country for women.

Moving from the political capital to the financial capital, Mumbai, students of one of India's biggest tech institutes continue to speak out against extreme exam pressure after a 20-year-old allegedly took their own life last week. However, the institute's faculty are also protesting, backing a professor who was suspended from his deanship as a result.

On the global front, we have India's Foreign Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar attending the 81st  United Nations General Assembly in New York where he has met several European partners on the sidelines of the event. Meanwhile, in Texas, a large idol of a Hindu deity has emerged as a point of debate ahead of the US midterm elections. 

Stay tuned for all of this and more!

entries.title: G7 demands Houthis 'immediately' cease Saudi strikes
entries.summary: The G7 nations have accused Yemen's Houthi rebels of targeting civilian shipping near Saudi Arabia. UK PM Andy Burnham said he will offer "time-limited" and "defensive" military support to repel the attacks.
entries.content:
Saudi Arabia

G7 demands Houthis 'immediately' cease Saudi strikes

September 22, 2026

The G7 nations have accused Yemen's Houthi rebels of targeting civilian shipping near Saudi Arabia. UK PM Andy Burnham said he will offer "time-limited" and "defensive" military support to repel the attacks.

The foreign ministers of G7 nations on Monday denounced Houthi attacks in Yemen and against Saudi Arabia while urging Iran to end its support, including arming, of the rebels,

"We condemn in ‌the strongest terms the unacceptable continued strikes carried out by ‌the Houthis in Yemen ‌and against the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia," the ministers of Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States said in a joint statement, after meeting on the sidelines of the UNGA.

The statement called on the Houthis to "immediately cease all military actions, all threats and attacks against civilian shipping, and to return to the political process in good faith."

UK offers air-to-air refuelling assistance to Saudi aircraft

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has agreed to give limited military support to Saudi Arabia as the Middle Eastern kingdom continues to face attacks from Yemen's Houthi rebels.

Britain's Royal Air Force (RAF) will provide "defensive" air-to-air refuelling for Saudi aircraft, Burham told reporters on Monday as he travelled to New York for the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA).

The prime minister said that the UK had "received a request" from Saudi Arabia for military support.

The British leader said he was "acting to secure the interests of Britain and the wider region, because of course Saudi Arabia has been experiencing attack, is looking at potential further disruption, and we need to keep those pathways [for oil] open."

What do we know about the UK's 'defensive' military support to Saudi Arabia?

Reports cited UK officials as saying that the agreement, which is likely to start within days, will be time-capped and could last for "weeks".

The mission would involve the use of the RAF's Voyager tanker and is in addition to the UK Sky Sabre air defence system which is already deployed in Saudi Arabia.

The UK mission will support Saudi jets in defending the country from drone and missile attacks rather than supporting strikes against the Iran-backed Houthis, the PA news agency reported.

Escalating tensions between Houthis and Saudi Arabia

Since 2015, Saudi Arabia has led a military coalition backing Yemen's internationally recognized government in its fight against the Houthis.

In July this year, a 2022 truce between the rebels and Saudi Arabia crumbled after the Houthis allowed an Iranian plane to land in Yemen's capital Sanaa, which defied the Saudis' control over Yemeni airspace.

On Saturday,  a Houthi attack on Riyadh was the first to target the Saudi capital in years.

The Houthis have also declared a blockade on Saudi shipping in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait  — a crucial global shipping route —  and the Red Sea.

Apart from Saudi-linked vessels, oil facilities inside Saudi Arabia — one of the world's top oil exporters — have also come under fire from Houthi drones and missiles.

Edited by: Rana Taha
